title: The Dark Cinema
briefing: Sofia, 15, walks from a sunny lobby into a dark movie theatre. At first she can't see the seats at all and trips on a step. Fifteen minutes later she can see faces and steps easily — in exactly the same dim light.
question: What changed in fifteen minutes — the theatre, or Sofia's eyes?

clues.title: Blind for a minute
clues.text: In the first minute she can't see the seats at all and trips on a step. Her eyes feel fine — there's just nothing to see.
clues.shows: eyes that are not yet ready for dim light

clues.title: Big pupils
clues.text: By the glow of her phone, her friend sees that Sofia's pupils have gone wide within a few seconds of walking in.
clues.shows: the pupils opening fully within seconds

clues.title: Better and better
clues.text: After five minutes she can see the steps; after fifteen she can read faces in the dim glow. The lights haven't changed.
clues.shows: her vision improving for many minutes after her pupils were already wide

clues.title: Her friend could see
clues.text: Her friend, who came in half an hour earlier, could see everything from the start. The room's lights stayed the same the whole time.
clues.shows: the light staying the same while only Sofia's eyes changed

hypotheses.text: Her eyes were tired from the bright lobby.
hypotheses.flaw: Tired eyes would get worse in the dark, not better — and she ended up seeing faces clearly.

hypotheses.text: Her pupils opened wider, and that is all that happened.
hypotheses.flaw: Her pupils were fully open within seconds, but her vision kept improving for fifteen minutes after that — something slower was also going on.

hypotheses.text: Two things happened: her pupils opened wide in seconds, and over many minutes the light-sensing cells at the back of her eyes rebuilt the pigment that bright light had used up, making them far more sensitive.
The theatre turned the lights up after the film started.
hypotheses.flaw: The lights never changed — her friend, who had been there for half an hour, could see fine from the start.

prediction.prompt: Sofia stays in the dark theatre for twenty minutes. How does her eyes' sensitivity to dim light change over that time?

second.question: And how long do her pupils take to finish opening?

concepts.label: pupils open quickly
concepts.hint: What happened to the black centres of her eyes, and how fast?

concepts.label: light-sensing cells
concepts.hint: Which part of the eye actually detects light?

concepts.label: pigment is rebuilt
concepts.hint: What does bright light use up, and what happens to it in the dark?

concepts.label: it takes many minutes
concepts.hint: How long did her vision keep improving?

concepts.label: eyes become more sensitive
concepts.hint: What is the word for eyes getting better at seeing in dim light?

transfer.context: Wei goes outside at night to look at the stars. At first he sees only a few; after twenty minutes away from his phone screen he sees hundreds.
options: More stars came out as the night went on.
His phone screen was blocking his view.
He was getting sleepy and imagining them.
His eyes rebuilt their light-sensing pigment in the dark, becoming far more sensitive over many minutes.
transfer.retryHint: Same sky, better view after waiting — which of Sofia's clues showed vision improving for many minutes?
transfer.explanation: The stars were there all along. Over twenty minutes in the dark, the light-sensing cells in Wei's eyes rebuilt the pigment his bright phone screen had used up, so fainter and fainter stars became visible — the same slow change that let Sofia see faces in the theatre.

takeaway: Your eyes adjust to the dark in two steps: pupils open wide in seconds, then the light-sensing cells slowly rebuild their pigment over many minutes, making you far more sensitive to dim light.
